China.polity: Northern Zhou, then Sui (581–618) and Tang (618–); Tibetan kingdom of Songtsen Gampo in the west
China.summary: Yang Jian (Emperor Wen) founded the Sui in 581 and reunified China by conquering the south in 589. His son Yangdi (r. 604–618) built the Grand Canal but exhausted the realm with failed wars against Goguryeo. Yangdi was assassinated in 618 and Li Yuan founded the Tang. His son Taizong seized power in 626, and in 630 Tang forces destroyed the Eastern Turkic khaganate. Songtsen Gampo expanded Tibet.

events.t: Sui armies capture Nanjing and conquer the south, reunifying China under Emperor Wen after three centuries of division.
Yangdi becomes emperor; his reign sees the building of the Grand Canal linking the Yangtze and Yellow rivers.
Yangdi personally leads a huge invasion of Goguryeo, which is crushed at the Salsu River; further campaigns in 613 and 614 also fail.
The Eastern Turkic ruler Shibi Qaghan besieges Yangdi at Yanmen, fuelling the rebellions that bring down the Sui.
Yangdi is assassinated; Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, founds the Tang dynasty and reigns as Gaozu.
Li Shimin kills his brothers, including the heir Li Jiancheng, in a coup; Gaozu abdicates and Li Shimin reigns as Taizong.
Songtsen Gampo is crowned king of Tibet; he later extends his rule to Nepal and parts of India and China.
Tang general Li Jing destroys the Eastern Turkic khaganate in surprise raids; his subordinate Zhang Baoxiang captures the khagan Illig.

sources.title: H. İ. Erkoç, The Impact of General Li Jing's Military Thought on the Fall of the Eastern Türk Qaghanate
sources.publisher: Çanakkale Araştırmaları Türk Yıllığı 22 (2017), Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University

Taiwan.summary: Taiwan was home to Indigenous peoples whose ancestors had lived on the island for more than 10,000 years and who spoke Austronesian languages. Many scholars see Taiwan as the starting point of the Austronesian expansion, though this is debated. There was no state and no outside rule. Chinese records report an expedition in the early 7th century that brought Indigenous people back to China. Documentation is very thin.

events.t: A Chinese expedition brings several Indigenous people from Taiwan back to China; a follow-up mission gathers more information (date as given by Britannica).

sources.title: Human settlement history between Sunda and Sahul: a focus on East Timor (Timor-Leste) and the Pleistocenic mtDNA diversity

Japan.polity: Yamato court (Asuka period) under Empress Suiko, then Emperor Jomei
Japan.summary: The Yamato court ruled from Asuka. From 587 the Soga clan dominated government. Empress Suiko (r. 592–628) reigned with Prince Shotoku as regent. Buddhism was promoted and temples such as Shitennoji, Hokoji and Horyuji were built, while teachers and scholars from Baekje in Korea brought Chinese learning such as Confucian texts. Official embassies to Sui China began about 607.

events.t: The Soga clan establishes control of the government, holding it until 645; the rival Mononobe clan had resisted Buddhism.
Prince Shotoku becomes regent for Empress Suiko, Japan's first empress, and governs on her behalf until his death in 622.
The Seventeen Article Constitution, credited to Prince Shotoku, sets out Buddhist and Confucian principles of government.
Horyuji temple is completed, and Japan sends the first of many official embassies to the Sui court.
Death of Prince Shotoku.
Jomei becomes emperor, reigning until 641.

North Korea.summary: This land was the heart of Goguryeo, the northernmost of Korea's Three Kingdoms, ruled from Pyongyang since 427. Under King Yeongyang (r. 590–618) it repelled Sui invasions in 598 and 612–614, most famously when general Eulji Mundeok won a great victory at the Salsu River in 612. Many Goguryeo tombs were decorated with painted murals.

events.t: A Sui invasion of Goguryeo fails after the army runs short of supplies and meets heavy rains.
General Eulji Mundeok wins a great victory over a huge Sui army at the Salsu River.
After a failed attack in 613, a further Sui campaign in 614 is also repelled.
King Yeongnyu succeeds Yeongyang, reigning until 642.
Goguryeo builds a defensive wall some 480 km long to deter further Chinese invasions.

sources.title: List of Rulers of Korea (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

South Korea.polity: Silla (southeast) and Baekje (southwest), two of Korea's Three Kingdoms
South Korea.summary: The south was divided between Silla, ruled from Geumseong (Gyeongju), which had absorbed the Gaya confederation by 562, and Baekje in the southwest, ruled from Sabi (Buyeo) since 538. They had been enemies since Silla seized the lower Han River valley in the 550s. Both had made Buddhism a state religion; Baekje exported much of its culture to Japan. Jinpyeong of Silla (r. 579–632) was succeeded by his daughter Seondeok.

events.t: King Jinpyeong begins a long reign in Silla.
King Mu takes the throne of Baekje, reigning until 641.
Seondeok succeeds her father Jinpyeong, becoming the first female sovereign in ancient Korea.

sources.title: List of Rulers of Korea (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Myanmar.polity: Pyu city-kingdoms (Sri Ksetra, Halin, Beikthano and others)
Myanmar.summary: The Pyu, speakers of Tibeto-Burman languages, held city-kingdoms in the Irrawaddy valley from about the 1st century BCE to the 9th century CE. Their brick-walled, moated cities, such as Sri Ksetra, Halin and Beikthano, stood in irrigated land in the dry zone, with monumental Buddhist stupas. Buddhism and other Indian influences were strong, and a trade route linked them to China and India. Evidence is mainly archaeological.

events.t: Pyu walled cities such as Sri Ksetra, Halin and Beikthano are in use, with Buddhist stupas and irrigated farmland.

Thailand.polity: Dvaravati (Mon kingdom) in the lower Chao Phraya valley; other local communities
Thailand.summary: Central Thailand saw the rise of Dvaravati, the first Mon kingdom in what is now Thailand. Centred in the lower Chao Phraya River valley, it emerged as an independent state late in the 6th century and spread Indian cultural influence. It was rarely politically dominant and lived in the shadow of stronger neighbours. Evidence for this period is limited.

events.t: Dvaravati emerges as an independent Mon kingdom in the lower Chao Phraya valley, late in the 6th century.

Laos.polity: Early Khmer polities in the Champasak region of the south
Laos.summary: Southern Laos, on the Champasak plain beside the Mekong, lay within the early Khmer world; Wat Phu was one of the important Khmer centres of the 7th century. UNESCO dates the planned riverside city of Shrestrapura there to the 5th–7th centuries, and the origins of the Vat Phou temple complex to the 7th century.

events.t: Shrestrapura, a planned city on the Mekong near Vat Phou (5th–7th centuries), is an early Khmer centre.

sources.title: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape

Cambodia.polity: Chenla, an early Khmer kingdom (capital Ishanapura)
Cambodia.summary: By the 7th century Khmer people lived along the Mekong, divided among warring kingdoms whose art and culture were strongly influenced by India. Sambor Prei Kuk, identified as Ishanapura, was the capital of Chenla, which flourished in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. Its brick temples, Sanskrit and Old Khmer inscriptions and sculpture laid foundations for later Khmer art.

events.t: Ishanapura (Sambor Prei Kuk), capital of Chenla, flourishes in the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

sources.title: Temple Zone of Sambor Prei Kuk, Archaeological Site of Ancient Ishanapura

Vietnam.polity: Annam region in the north; Champa kingdom; Khmer lands in the Mekong delta
Vietnam.summary: In the early 7th century Sui armies campaigned in the region, taking territory from Annam and from the kingdom of Champa; they defeated war elephants with crossbows, but many northern soldiers died of malaria. The Mekong delta in the far south lay within the Khmer world.

events.t: Sui armies take territory from Annam and Champa, routing war elephants with crossbows (early 7th century; exact dates vary).

Malaysia.polity: Small Indianised Malay kingdoms (notably Langkasuka); Iron Age communities in Sarawak and Sabah
Malaysia.summary: The Malay Peninsula held perhaps 30 small Indianised states during the 1st millennium CE, known mainly from Chinese sources; the most important, Langkasuka, controlled much of the north. Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism shaped court culture, and major temple ruins survive around Kedah Peak. Sarawak had entered the Iron Age by about 600 and traded with China. Srivijaya's loose control of the region came later, from the 7th century.

events.t: Sarawak has entered the Iron Age; sites in the Sarawak River delta show ironworking and trade with China and mainland Southeast Asia.

Brunei.polity: Austronesian coastal communities trading with China
Brunei.summary: The early history of Brunei is obscure. Encyclopaedia Britannica states that it was already trading with and paying tribute to China in the 6th century CE. Little else is known for this period, and there is little archaeological evidence.

events.t: Brunei is recorded as trading with and paying tribute to China in the 6th century.

Indonesia.polity: Small Indianised Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms on Java and Sumatra; many local communities
Indonesia.summary: Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms based on Indian ideas of the state had arisen in Sumatra and, somewhat later, Java. Tarumanegara, established about the 5th century, is the oldest recorded kingdom of west Java. Srivijaya, the great Sumatran maritime power based at Palembang, flourished from the 7th century; it is first recorded when the Chinese pilgrim I-ching visited in 671, after this period. Evidence for these decades is thin.

events.t: Small Indianised kingdoms on Java and Sumatra trade by sea; Srivijaya will rise at Palembang later in the 7th century.

sources.title: Indonesia: The Malay kingdom of Srivijaya-Palembang

Philippines.polity: Independent Austronesian communities without central government
Philippines.summary: The islands were home to diverse peoples with little contact with each other and no centralised government. Later accounts suggest lowland people lived in kin groups called barangays, each led by a datu. In northern Luzon, rice terraces had been built about 2,000 years earlier. Chinese and Indian influence was slight; the first recorded contact with Chinese traders dates to 982. No written records survive from this period.

events.t: Island communities live by farming, hunting and fishing; no written records or dated events survive.

Timor-Leste.summary: Timor had been inhabited for more than 42,000 years. Its early settlers are linked with non-Austronesian (Papuan) languages, while Austronesian speakers arrived in eastern Indonesia and Timor about 4,000 years ago. Its people today are of Papuan, Malay and Polynesian origin. There was no state and no written record, and no dated events are known for this period.

events.t: Village communities continue; no dated events are recorded.

sources.title: Human settlement history between Sunda and Sahul: a focus on East Timor (Timor-Leste) and the Pleistocenic mtDNA diversity

Papua New Guinea.summary: New Guinea's highlands had been farmed for thousands of years: at Kuk swamp, wetlands were drained with ditches dug with wooden tools, and bananas, taro and yams were grown. Papuan-speaking groups were the older population. Austronesian languages were spoken mainly on coasts and in the Bismarck Archipelago, where Lapita people had settled by 2000 BCE. No written records exist.

events.t: Highland farming and coastal communities continue; evidence is archaeological only.

Australia.polity: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples (many distinct nations)
Australia.summary: Australia was home to many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups, each with its own culture, language, beliefs and practices. Current research suggests they had lived on the continent for upwards of 60,000 years. Torres Strait Islanders lived on the islands between Cape York and New Guinea. No specific events can be dated for this period.

events.t: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies continue long-established ways of life; no specific dated events.

sources.title: First Peoples of Australia
sources.publisher: Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS)

New Zealand.summary: No humans lived in New Zealand in this period. Most evidence indicates that the first settlers, Polynesians from East Polynesia, arrived by canoe around 1250–1300. Rat bones once dated to about 50–150 CE suggested an earlier visit, but most scientists now think those dates are inaccurate.

events.t: The islands remain uninhabited; Polynesian settlement comes around 1250–1300.

sources.title: When was New Zealand first settled?
sources.publisher: Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand

Fiji.summary: Fiji's first settlers arrived from other Pacific islands at least 3,500 years ago; Lapita people had spread into West Polynesia from about 1000 BCE. Their descendants lived in island communities with no written records, and the period is known only through archaeology.

events.t: Island communities continue; no dated events are known.

sources.title: When was New Zealand first settled?
sources.publisher: Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand

Vanuatu.summary: Archaeological evidence shows that by 1300 BCE islands in northern Vanuatu had been settled by people of the Lapita culture from Melanesian islands to the west, followed by successive waves of migrants. A highly stratified society developed in central Vanuatu only around 1200. There are no written records for this period.

events.t: Island communities continue; no specific dated events are known.

Solomon Is..polity: Independent Papuan- and Austronesian-speaking island communities
Solomon Is..summary: People had lived in the Solomon Islands for thousands of years. Papuan (non-Austronesian) languages are spoken as far east as the Solomons, and Lapita people began spreading to the islands from about 1600 BCE. Communities farmed and fished in small villages. No written records exist for this period.

events.t: Island communities continue; evidence is archaeological only.

sources.title: Human settlement history between Sunda and Sahul: a focus on East Timor (Timor-Leste) and the Pleistocenic mtDNA diversity

New Caledonia.polity: Independent Melanesian communities (ancestors of the Kanak)
New Caledonia.summary: New Caledonia had long been settled by Melanesians (Britannica gives about 3000 BCE). The Lapita pottery culture takes its name from a site here. Apart from rare Polynesian voyagers, the islanders were probably cut off from outside contact until the late 18th century. There are no written records, and the period is known only through archaeology.

events.t: Melanesian communities continue; no dated events are known.

Antarctica.summary: Antarctica had no native population and no recorded human visits before the 19th century. Rarotongan oral tradition tells of Ui-te-Rangiora sailing south to a frozen region around 650, but the continent itself was first sighted in 1820, by Russian, British or American sailors.

Fr. S. Antarctic Lands.summary: The Kerguelen and Crozet islands in the southern Indian Ocean had no human inhabitants. They were unknown until French navigators discovered them in 1772: Kerguelen-Trémarec found the Kerguelen Islands and Marion-Dufresne found the Crozet Islands.

events.t: No humans live on the islands.
